newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's Ruiz says low tax receipts spur crackdown.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's Ruiz says low tax receipts spur crackdown.

text.p: A slump in tax receipts in the first half of 1996 has forced the government to launch a high profile crack-down on tax fraud and evasion, a top Finance Ministry official said on Friday.
Speaking after a Mexican media magnate surrendered to authorities on charges of tax fraud, Tomas Ruiz, undersecretary for revenues at the Finance Ministry told Reuters more heads would roll.
"It's to send a message that people have to obey the law and pay their taxes," he said.
According to Ruiz, income tax receipts in the first half of 1996 fell 18 percent compared with the same period last year, and payments of value added tax were off up to 35 percent.
Though the budget has remained in surplus because of a windfall rise in oil revenues, he said evasion -- described in Mexico as "the national sport" -- was reaching alarming levels.
"We have seen a notable relaxation in terms of paying," he said, and this despite government efforts to help people pay taxes in the face of Mexico's economic crisis last year.

Though he appeared to take a softer line on evasion, Ruiz said tax fraud would not be tolerated. On Friday, Juan Francisco Ealy Ortiz, editor of El Universal newspaper, was held on charges he had defrauded tax authorities of $5.4 million over the last two years.

Other top figures snagged by the unprecedented tax crackdown include Julio Csar Chvez, Mexico's boxing hero. Diego Fernndez de Cevallos, a former presidential candidate for the opposition National Action Party, has also been accused by pro-government media of bilking the taxman.
Ruiz said two other important businessmen were also being targetted, but he declined to name them.

The official insisted there were no political criteria involved in deciding who to hunt down, and he roundly denied charges raised principally by El Universal that the charges against Ealy Ortiz were an assault on press freedom.
"It was not directed against a newspaper nor against the media," he said.
